We need to talk about that ‘originality’ panic. You know the one—staring at a blank screen, convinced your professor wants you to reinvent the wheel. Spoiler: they don't. In fact, trying to invent a brand new theory usually leads to an unsubstantiated opinion piece that hits a wall during grading.

Slide 2: The Trap. You’re stressing over novelty, but your marker is looking for depth. 

Slide 3: The Fix. Instead of inventing, try synthesizing. Take two opposing empirical studies, pull them apart, critique their sampling, and build a conclusion that actually has teeth. That’s how you move from a 54% to a 78%+.

Stop trying to be a genius and start being a scholar. If your argument feels a bit shaky, let’s look at it together. 

Save this for your next draft.

copy.facebook:
I see so many students burning out because they think an essay needs to be a ground-breaking piece of philosophy. Let’s clear the air: your professor is grading your ability to engage with the literature, not your ability to invent a new one.

If you’re stuck in the 50s, it’s usually because you’re offering opinions instead of evidence. Here is the shift you need to make:

• Stop: Trying to create a 'novel model' from thin air.
• Start: Contrasting two major studies in your field.
• Stop: Writing what you think.
• Start: Critiquing the sampling methods or limitations of the research you're citing.
• Stop: The Turnitin panic.
• Start: Building a justified, evidence-based position.

It’s a simple shift, but it’s the difference between a pass and a high distinction. If you’ve got a draft that feels like it’s missing that 'academic edge,' send me a message on WhatsApp at +91 95098 93638 and let’s tighten up your argument structure together.
